title: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Cellular Automata” (from p. 170), p. 179. Scope: three-dimensional cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-05: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Representative ensembles can be simulated and compared with standard computation. Current catalogs and feasible searches cover only tiny, noncanonical parts of the three-dimensional space, so the dimensionality-independent generalization remains partial.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample matched one-, two-, and three-dimensional cellular-automaton rule ensembles and classify trajectories using a preregistered behavior taxonomy and dimension-normalized metrics. Compare class coverage and complexity prevalence across dimensions.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Matched random rules across dimensions are encoding-dependent.

Basic kinds of behavior lacks an exhaustive formal taxonomy.

Three-dimensional rule spaces are combinatorially large.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.42
operationalizability: 0.48
analysis feasibility: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Small three-dimensional rules are straightforward to simulate, and the examples in the book can be recomputed and labeled with the same taxonomy used in lower dimensions. That tests the claim on a sample. It does not cover three-dimensional rules in general, and the phrase 'basic kinds' is elastic enough that a novel phenomenon can be filed as a detail rather than a counterexample.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate a sample of three-dimensional cellular automata with 6-neighbor and 26-neighbor rules and classify them against the one- and two-dimensional behavior types. A behavior that cannot be placed in those types would challenge 'the same basic kinds'; a sample that stays within them supports the claim for that sample.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'The same basic kinds' can absorb new phenomena by calling them minor, which weakens refutation.

Three-dimensional rule space is too large to exhaust, and printed or rendered samples emphasize symmetric cases.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.6
discriminating power: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.55
